tldr: A dating profile is the first version of ourselves that strangers see. In this study, 20 experienced dating-app users in China built a profile in front of the researchers and explained each choice. They picked photos to spark curiosity, protect their privacy and signal shared interests, and they shaped profiles to mirror both an idealized self and the partner they hoped to attract.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: Semi-structured interviews with live profile construction

contributions: A step-by-step account of how experienced users build dating profiles, especially how they select and order photos.

A set of visual strategies: limiting facial display to stimulate imagination, hiding identifying details to protect privacy, choosing the first photo carefully, and using everyday photos as conversation starters.
Four persona construction strategies, and a cyclical paradigm in which users show the traits they value in a partner to attract people who share them.
Evidence of an asymmetry between how users present themselves and how they judge others, for example hiding their own faces while judging others mainly by appearance.
Design implications for dating platforms: two-stage self-presentation, searchable matching attributes such as niche hobbies, and trust built on visible common ground.

sections.heading: Motivation
paragraphs: A dating profile decides how people present themselves to potential partners and what they choose to hide. Prior work has mostly examined the authenticity of dating profiles, but less is known about how users choose text and images, or how concealment and embellishment affect how profiles are perceived.

The paper defines “strategy” as the deliberate and conscious methods people use to manage self-presentation on dating platforms, mainly by selecting and organizing photos and text. Three research questions guided the study.
bullets: RQ1: What strategies do people adopt when selecting images for their dating profiles?
RQ2: How do people use dating profiles to present themselves and for what purpose?
RQ3: What key factors may influence people’s perception of others’ profiles?

sections.heading: Method
paragraphs: Twenty native Chinese speakers aged 22 to 33 (mean 25.0), each with experience of at least one dating app, were recruited through WeChat and Xiaohongshu. Seventeen identified as heterosexual and three as homosexual. Their education ranged from undergraduate to doctorate, and seven had lived or studied abroad. Interviews lasted 30 to 60 minutes and were held in Mandarin via Tencent Meeting, Feishu, WeChat or in person.

Participants logged in to a researcher-created Tinder account and built a new profile step by step: text, filters such as gender and relationship intent, and six photos. They were asked to think aloud while researchers probed their reasons, and profiles were never uploaded. As participants focused mainly on photos, the interviews shifted toward photo choices. Four researchers coded the transcripts independently and reached three themes: visual aspects of photo selection, persona construction strategy, and perception of others’ profiles.

figures.caption: Interview process: informed consent and demographics, a semi-structured interview on three topics, then recording results and summarizing insights.

sections.heading: Photos That Spark Curiosity and Protect Privacy
paragraphs: Many participants cared more about the atmosphere of a photo than about showing their face. They used body language, lighting, negative space and blur to add mystery. P3 avoided clear front-face photos and put any flattering shot at the end, so that only people who swiped through would see her face. P8 limited her face to a small part of the frame: “my face could only occupy one grid.” Others avoided full-face photos for fear of being recognized by friends or family on the same app.

Photo order was also strategic. Because apps show only the first photo at first (P9), the first photo served as the profile’s “facade”. Some participants followed a striking photo with humorous or quirky ones to reduce the distance that good looks can create. P14 chose sports photos to attract people who share that interest, and several participants preferred everyday photos, such as food, as light conversation starters.

figures.caption: Photos uploaded by P8: (a) her face is not shown and much of the frame is blank; (b) a swing photo conveys body language; (c) her face occupies one of nine grid cells.

sections.heading: Constructing a Persona
paragraphs: Participants used four persona strategies: complying with external expectations, idealizing themselves to meet inner needs, expressing themselves authentically through lifestyle, and crafting an engaging persona to capture attention. P1, who had used dating apps in both China and Sweden, avoided mentioning her body size in China but listed it in Sweden, where standards differ. P4, seeking a serious relationship, chose photos with less skin exposure in China to avoid signaling interest in only sexual relationships.

Idealization was sometimes unconscious. P12 listed a lower weight than his real one and said, “It’s not intentional. It may be subconscious.” He also listed a more prestigious university than the one he attended. Others aimed for authenticity by weaving hobbies into daily life, such as P8 photographing scenery together with her own sketch. To appear intriguing, P4 mentioned niche hobbies like astrology and wrote “only talk until 10 pm”, P10 chose back-view photos, and P3 found that photos with very different styles from different periods made people curious.

figures.caption: Example photos from participants’ statements: (a) scenery and one’s own sketch, showing a talent indirectly (P8); (b) a landscape photo versus a photo with people (P4); (c) photos with very different appearances from different periods, which aroused curiosity (P3).

sections.heading: Judging Others’ Profiles
paragraphs: When viewing others’ profiles, participants looked for authenticity. They distrusted photos that looked “cut out of a magazine”, sets of photos that were inconsistent with each other, blurry or low-quality images, and displays of luxury brands and cars. P13 checked such photos with Baidu image search.

Most participants formed first impressions from physical attributes, especially appearance and height. Small cues also mattered: P1 was drawn to photos with animals, and unique text caught the attention of P2 and P15. Participants disagreed about text. P3 felt that “photos are more believable than words” because they are harder to create, yet also said that words can reveal subtler traits than photos.

sections.heading: Discussion: Showing What We Value
paragraphs: Unlike Facebook connections, dating matches rarely share a social network, so participants built common ground through photos of daily life, such as a favorite restaurant a match could visit with them. Participants also built profiles that mirrored both an “ideal self” and an “ideal partner”. The authors conceptualize this as a cyclical paradigm: “I show what I value; I attract people who like what I show; I discern those I attract whether have traits I value.”

Drawing on Goffman’s “front stage” and “backstage”, the authors suggest a third mode: users believed they were presenting their backstage selves but were already on the front stage, acting as their own audience. The study also found a double standard. Participants hid their own faces yet judged others mainly by appearance, used blurred photos for privacy yet read blur in others’ photos as a sign of falsehood, and demanded authenticity while exaggerating themselves “to an acceptable extent”.

figures.caption: The cyclical paradigm when users create profiles: “I show what I value; I attract people who like what I show; I discern those I attract whether have traits I value.”

sections.heading: Design Implications
paragraphs: The authors propose three directions for dating platforms that support self-expression while limiting inaccurate information and protecting privacy.
bullets: Two-stage presentation: show a curated first layer, then reveal more as the relationship progresses (for example, after a certain amount of chat time). This could help users worried about being judged, including people with “invisible” disabilities and transgender users.
More precise matchmaking: identify matching attributes such as niche hobbies from profiles and make them searchable, while keeping the number of choices manageable.
Reliable trust: visualize shared cultural connections, for example cities visited, restaurants reviewed or favorite animations drawn from users’ other social media accounts.

sections.heading: Limitations & Follow-up Work
paragraphs: All participants were college-educated young Chinese users, so the findings may not generalize to other groups. The data were self-reported and may be affected by social desirability and researcher bias. The study also gave limited attention to profile text, differences between platforms, and image editing.

The findings later informed Carbon Copy, an interactive installation by the same team. It is a fake dating platform in which ChatGPT writes profile text modeled on the patterns of real users from this study, and Stable Diffusion generates matching images of consistent AI personas.
